 Key Points 
 Penn admitted 3,570 of 72,544 first-year applicants for fall 2025, and 68% of the students it admitted enrolled. Early decision accounted for 1,266 of those admits, equal to 52% of the 2,420-student first-year class.
 Under the Quaker Commitment, families earning up to $75,000 with typical assets pay nothing for tuition, fees, housing and dining, and families earning up to $200,000 pay no tuition. Penn's financial aid packages use grants instead of student loans.
 16% of the class of 2025 took out student loans. Those who borrowed left with an average of $33,655.

 Is Penn Worth It? The College Investor Rating
 A Penn earns an A overall, scoring 86 out of 100. Low-income families get an A, middle-income families get an A, and high-income families paying full price get a B. Its strongest marks come from payoff, graduation rate and student debt. Price pulls the score down. Whether college is worth it depends on how much you spend .

 What Penn Weighs In Admissions
 Penn rates course rigor, academic GPA, essay, recommendations and character as very important. Demonstrated interest counts for nothing: campus visits won't change your odds. Alumni relationships are considered.

 What Will Penn Actually Cost Your Family?
 The average Penn student receiving financial aid paid $29,577 a year after grants.
 That's against a sticker price of $92,288 a year. Under the Quaker Commitment, families earning up to $75,000 with typical assets pay nothing for tuition, fees, housing and dining, and families earning up to $200,000 pay no tuition. Penn's financial aid packages use grants instead of student loans. Penn is one of a growing number of colleges offering free tuition by family income .

 How Penn Meets Financial Need
 Penn reports meeting 100% of demonstrated financial need on average. In 2024-2025, 4,575 of Penn's 9,974 full-time undergraduates had financial need, and their average need-based grant was $70,215. Penn determines financial need with both the FAFSA and the CSS Profile , so how your assets are counted affects what you pay. Penn awards essentially no merit scholarships.
 Grants made up 95% of Penn's need-based financial aid in 2024-2025. The rest came from student jobs, including Federal Work-Study, and $1,952,112 in student loans.

 Red Flag Families Still Borrow At A School That Meets Full Financial Need
 Penn reports meeting 100% of financial need. Families borrowed anyway: in 2024-2025, parents took out $14,259,789 in parent loans, including Parent PLUS loans, and students borrowed $18,742,989 in student loans. In the class of 2025, 102 graduates left with private student loans averaging $73,246.
 The "100% of financial need met" figure leaves out Parent PLUS loans, unsubsidized federal student loans and private student loans, because those loans replace what the school expects the family to pay. Before you commit, read your financial aid award letter line by line and appeal the financial aid award if the number doesn't fit your budget.

 Does A Penn Degree Pay Off?
 Generally, yes. That's why Penn earns an A from The College Investor .
 Penn students earn a median of $121,687 ten years after starting college, and 94% out-earn a typical high school graduate. 11% take out federal student loans, and the typical borrower leaves owing $15,000, about 12% of one year's pay. Earnings still depend heavily on major: Computer And Information Sciences graduates earned a median of $241,380 four years after graduating, compared with $68,435 for Biology graduates.

 How We Graded Penn
 The overall grade weighs payoff, price, graduation and student debt. Price counts what low-income families pay (5 points), what middle-income families pay (10 points) and the sticker price high-income families pay (10 points). Each income grade swaps in that family's price alone.

 Sources And Methodology The College Investor Rating scores every four-year college from 0 to 100 on payoff (30%), price (25%), graduation (20%) and student debt (25%) using U.S. Department of Education College Scorecard data. An earnings floor and a financial health check can cap the grade at D, and a financial aid check flags concerns without changing it. Price is judged on its own, without earnings. The grade measures financial return for families, not teaching quality, campus life or a school's mission.
 Notes On The Data
 Low-income families earn under $48,000. Middle-income families earn $48,000 to $110,000. Their prices are federal averages for first-time, full-time students who received financial aid.
 High-income families are those who get no grant aid, so they pay the sticker price (cost of attendance).
 Paying full price is the share of undergraduates who received no grant aid from any source in 2022-23, from the Education Department's IPEDS survey. The chance of merit aid divides merit scholarship recipients by full-time undergraduates without financial need, from the Common Data Set.
 Earnings by major are medians four years after graduation. Majors with too few graduates for the government to report earnings are left out. Debt by major is median federal student loan debt among borrowers.
 Admissions, financial aid and class of 2025 student loan figures come from the Penn Common Data Set 2025-2026. Student loan debt at graduation excludes Parent PLUS and other parent loans, and students who transferred in.
 The calculator uses federal net price averages. Borrowing up to the $27,000 federal limit for dependent undergraduates uses the 2026-27 undergraduate rate of 6.52%, and anything above it uses the 9.07% Parent PLUS rate. Parent PLUS loans are capped at $20,000 a year and $65,000 per student. See all federal student loan interest rates . Penn's own net price calculator gives a personal figure, and College Aid Pro can compare costs across schools .
 Data years: Earnings follow students who started college in 2011-12 and 2012-13, measured 10 years later. Net price and borrowing rates are for 2024-25. Graduation rates follow students who started in fall 2019. Median debt covers borrowers who left school in fiscal 2024 and 2025. Full-price shares are for 2022-23.
 Work at Penn? If a figure looks wrong, send us the source and our editors will review it.
 Sources: Penn Common Data Set 2025-2026 . U.S. Department of Education College Scorecard , data updated November 2, 2026. News from The College Investor.
